Overview In October 2025, Cyble identified GhostBat RAT being distributed through MiningDropper and targeting Android users in India. We have since continued to track related activity and investigate malicious applications impersonating India’s mParivahan and eChallan services. This research uncovered a broader Android threat ecosystem that we track as GhostX, along with significantly evolved variants of GhostBat RAT. The most recent GhostBat RAT variant demonstrates a notable increase in capability and operational flexibility. It uses Firebase Remote Config to dynamically manage command-and-control (C&C) infrastructure and to enable or disable individual malware modules without requiring APK redistribution. This variant also implements a sophisticated Ghost Overlay technique targeting legitimate Google Pay and MobiKwik PIN-entry interfaces. Instead of displaying a conventional fake login page, the malware places transparent accessibility overlays over the legitimate application’s keypad, records the victim’s touch selections, and replays the same interaction into the genuine application. Additionally, the malware implements a PIN-capture capability through keylogging, targeting 60 Android applications across India’s banking, UPI, wallet, fintech, and digital payment ecosystem. The malware’s delivery and packing mechanisms have evolved considerably across the samples analyzed. We identified at least six distinct loader or dropper implementations, including: Native AES-CBC-protected APK containers Custom SPKZ/SPK1 payload formats Java-based in-memory DEX loaders Remote APK downloaders Multi-stage XOR/AES loaders A newer native libnetbridge.so loader using multiple cryptographic, transformation, compression, and custom container stages before recovering the final payload This diversification suggests continued investment in defeating static detection and complicating automated malware extraction. GhostBat RAT is primarily distributed via smishing messages that contain malicious links. When victims follow these links, they are redirected to phishing pages that impersonate either the legitimate Parivahan service or a Google Play-style application download page and are encouraged to install a fraudulent mParivahan APK (see Figures 2 and 3). During our investigation, we also repeatedly observed GitHub repositories and GitHub-hosted assets being used to distribute malicious APKs, providing attackers with readily available public hosting infrastructure. Figure 2 – Fake Google Play Store-style mParivahan installation website Figure 3 – Fake mParivahan website prompting to download APK file Discovery of the GhostX Ecosystem The GhostX investigation began with the discovery of multiple Android applications impersonating India’s mParivahan and eChallan ecosystem. Samples were collected from phishing infrastructure and public GitHub repositories containing APKs named or presented as mParivahan, vehicle-challan, traffic-enforcement, or other related government applications. Initial static analysis revealed that many of these APKs were only first-stage loaders. Their visible DEX code offered limited functionality, while the actual malware payload was either concealed within encrypted assets or retrieved later. After unpacking the applications to their final payloads, we identified multiple custom C&C infrastructures, Firebase projects, and overlapping Android surveillance and financial-fraud capabilities. A major breakthrough came from the analysis of a NextGen mParivahan sample whose unpacked payload contained the Firebase project identifier: ghostx-panel The exposed Firebase backend provided significantly greater visibility into the operator’s infrastructure and control workflow. The database contained structures including: clients bot_users admins admin_logins settings All_Users Verify_Device Analysis of the exposed GhostX backend revealed evidence of a structured operator-management layer beyond conventional malware C&C functionality. The database contained administrator and user records with role and account-status fields, a global session identifier, bot-user mappings, and dedicated admin_logins records containing device fingerprints, timestamps, and online status (see Figure 4). These artifacts indicate that GhostX incorporates an authentication and session management framework for operator-side access and management of compromised devices. The presence of distinct user, administrator, and bot-user roles suggests a multi-operator, service-oriented architecture. It raises the possibility that GhostX could support a Malware-as-a-Service-style operating model. Figure 4 – Exposed administrative records. During continued monitoring of the exposed infrastructure, we observed that SMS lure content, phishing URLs, vehicle registration numbers, and recipient phone numbers were repeatedly changing, indicating active operator-side campaign management rather than a static or abandoned database (see Figure 5). Similar eChallan-themed messages were also observed being received by users in the wild, further supporting the campaign's operational nature (see Figure 6). Figure 5 – Exposed SMS message configured to be sent to victims Figure 6 – Same SMSs are being received by the victims (Source – Twitter Post) One of the phishing URLs exposed through the GhostX infrastructure subsequently led us to a previously unseen GhostBat RAT variant, providing a direct investigative link among the backend control ecosystem, active phishing operations, and the malware's continued evolution. These findings led us to assess that GhostX is not a single Android malware family or standalone application. Instead, GhostX represents a broader operator-controlled ecosystem encompassing phishing infrastructure, backend services, Firebase-based configuration and command mechanisms, device-management functionality, and malware distribution. GhostBat RAT represents the Android implant operating within this ecosystem, with individual variants continuing to evolve across both delivery mechanisms and post-compromise capabilities. Technical Analysis Evolution of Droppers and Loaders GhostBat RAT has undergone continuous changes in its delivery and payload-protection mechanisms. Across the samples analyzed during the GhostX investigation, we identified multiple loader and dropper implementations designed to conceal the underlying malware payload, complicate static analysis, and reduce the effectiveness of hash- and signature-based detection. Although the recovered payloads demonstrate overlapping capabilities for surveillance, financial theft, and device control, the mechanisms used to deliver and recover them vary considerably across samples. Earlier variants relied on comparatively straightforward native loaders that decrypted embedded APK payloads using AES-CBC. Subsequent variants of Ghostbat RAT introduced XOR-encrypted custom containers, SPKZ/SPK1 packaging, split-APK delivery, dynamically loaded DEX components, and Java-based in-memory loaders. One variant moved away from embedded payload delivery entirely. It operated as a remote downloader, retrieving a second-stage APK from remote infrastructure, validating its SHA-256 hash, and installing it through Android's package installation framework. The most recent variant analyzed introduces a substantially more complex native loader implemented in libnetbridge.so. This loader combines multiple transformations, encryption, compression, and custom container stages before recovering the final GhostBat RAT payload. This diversification indicates continued modification of the delivery layer while broadly retaining the malware's post-compromise objectives. Consequently, detections that focus only on the outer APK, the encrypted asset name, or a single unpacking routine are unlikely to provide durable coverage. The GhostBat RAT loaders/droppers variants we observed are listed below: Figure 7 – GhostBat RAT Loader variants The most recent GhostBat RAT sample introduced a significantly more complex native unpacking mechanism. Unlike earlier variants that relied primarily on Java-based loaders or comparatively straightforward XOR/AES routines, this variant stores the encrypted payload inside an opaque application asset, assets/isti52q4, while most of the unpacking logic is implemented in the native library libnetbridge.so. The visible application code does not directly expose the final malicious functionality. Instead, execution transitions to the native loader, which processes the embedded asset through several sequential stages of transformation and decryption (see Figure 8). Figure 8 – Latest native dropper unpacking chain The first stage processes content within the encrypted asset file and derives values required for subsequent decoding. The resulting data is then passed through an RC4-like transformation before being processed through AES-256-GCM. This layered approach prevents the encrypted asset from being recovered using simple XOR or direct AES key extraction techniques that worked against earlier GhostBat RAT loaders. Following successful decryption, the loader recovers an MSZ1-formatted intermediate object that is decompressed using zlib. The decompressed data contains an MSP1 container that packages the final Android application components. The recovered payload consists of a split-APK application, including base.apk and split_config.dex.apk. The executable malware code is primarily contained within the recovered split configuration DEX. Unlike earlier samples, where the encrypted payload could be identified directly from ZIP headers or standard APK structures, the latest loader hides the final application behind several custom transformations before any recognizable Android package becomes available. This significantly increases the effort required for automated unpacking and reduces the effectiveness of simple asset-scanning techniques. Advanced GhostBat RAT Payload GhostBat RAT has evolved from an Android SMS and information stealer into a modular remote-access and Banking Trojan. Across the analyzed variants, the malware demonstrates capabilities for device profiling, SMS interception, remote SMS transmission, call-forwarding manipulation, payment-data theft, accessibility-based PIN capture, Firebase-driven command delivery, dynamic C&C configuration, and remote tunnelling. In the new GhostBat RAT variant, we observed the introduction of Android Accessibility Service abuse, a technique commonly associated with modern Android Banking Trojans. Earlier GhostBat RAT variants that we analyzed did not possess these capabilities during this investigation. The new variant uses Accessibility Service to monitor foreground applications, identify PIN-entry contexts, interact with application interfaces, and support two distinct credential-theft mechanisms: Ghost Overlay and targeted PIN/key-input capture. Once Accessibility Services access is granted, the malware monitors the foreground application and compares it against configured target lists. These targets can be managed through Firebase Remote Config, allowing operators to selectively activate credential-capture functionality when a targeted banking, UPI, wallet, or payment application is in use. Ghost Overlay The most notable capability introduced in this variant is the Ghost Overlay technique. Figure 9.1 – Ghost Overlay Attack Flow Unlike conventional Android overlay attacks that display a fake login or payment page over the legitimate application, GhostBat RAT does not need to replace the victim's banking interface. Instead, it places transparent accessibility overlay regions directly over the real PIN keypad displayed by the targeted application. The feature is controlled through Firebase Remote Config using: ghost_overlay_enabled ghost_overlay_packages Figure 9.2 – Ghost overlay initialization activity The default Ghost Overlay configuration targets the following Android packages: com.mobikwik_new com.google.android.apps.nbu.paisa com.google.android.apps.nbu.paisa.user Figure 10 – Target package list of Ghost Overlay activity When the malware detects one of these applications in the foreground and identifies a PIN-related activity, it creates a transparent keypad grid using Android’s TYPE_ACCESSIBILITY_OVERLAY. The overlay contains 12 touch regions matching the layout of a typical numeric PIN pad (see Figures 11 and 12): Figure 11 – Ghost PIN pad structure Figure 12 – Ghost overlay activity When the victim taps a digit on the legitimate Google Pay or MobiKwik PIN keypad, the transparent Ghost Overlay intercepts the touch event before it reaches the underlying application. The malware maps the touch coordinates to the corresponding keypad value and appends the resulting digit to an internal buffer used to reconstruct the PIN. To avoid interrupting the payment flow or alerting the victim, GhostBat RAT temporarily releases the affected overlay region and uses AccessibilityService.dispatchGesture() to reproduce the same tap at the corresponding screen coordinates (see Figure 13). As a result, the legitimate application receives the expected input and continues operating normally, while the malware records the victim's PIN in parallel. The same mechanism handles DEL and OK interactions, allowing the GhostBat RAT to update the captured digit sequence and detect when the PIN entry process has completed. This intercept-and-replay behavior enables the malware to observe PIN entry without presenting a fake Google Pay or MobiKwik interface. Figure 13 – dispatchGesture activity Once collected, the PIN is stored with metadata identifying the capture source as ghost_overlay and is subsequently queued for exfiltration over C&C “hxxps://api.cloudsettle[.]org/pin-data” (see Figure 14). Figure 14 – Storing captured Ghost PIN This technique is considerably stealthier than a conventional phishing overlay because the victim remains within the genuine financial application's interface throughout the interaction. GhostBat RAT effectively operates as an invisible intermediary, intercepting the victim's keypad interaction, recording the selected digits, and replaying those same touches into the legitimate application in near real time. Targeted Keylogging and PIN Capture In addition to the Ghost Overlay capability, the new GhostBat RAT variant implements a broader accessibility-based PIN/key-input capture mechanism targeting applications across India’s banking, UPI, wallet, fintech, and digital-payment ecosystem. Unlike the Ghost Overlay feature, which is specifically designed to intercept keypad touches in Google Pay and MobiKwik via transparent overlay regions, this functionality relies on Android Accessibility Service events to monitor user interactions across a much larger set of targeted applications. The default pin_target_packages configuration includes 60 Android package identifiers for financial applications used across India (see Figure 15). The target set includes applications associated with Google Pay, PhonePe, Paytm, MobiKwik, BHIM, SBI UPI, Axis Pay, BharatPe, CRED, Freecharge, PayZapp, Groww, Navi, Jupiter, OneCard, JioFinance, Samsung Pay, and several other banking and payment services. The complete list of targeted Android packages is provided in the Targeted Application List section. Once Accessibility Service is granted, GhostBat RAT monitors foreground activity and determines whether the currently running application(s) match an entry in pin_target_packages. The malware then evaluates the surrounding application and screen context before treating observed numeric input as potentially sensitive PIN information. Figure 15 – PIN target package list The malware also uses configurable PIN-length boundaries, pin_min_digits, and pin_min_digits to determine whether the reconstructed numeric sequence is consistent with an expected PIN. Unlike Ghost Overlay, the broader keylogging mechanism does not rely on a transparent keypad overlay. Instead, GhostBat RAT uses Accessibility Service events and UI context to identify and reconstruct PIN-like input across a wider set of targeted financial applications, giving the malware substantially broader coverage within India’s banking and digital payment ecosystem. The analyzed variant contains a dedicated worker responsible for handling captured PIN information, “PinUploadWorker”. Captured PINS are locally queued before being transmitted to the endpoint “/pin-data”. Figure 16 – Captured PIN upload activity The introduction of this capability substantially expands the financial targeting of GhostBat RAT. Earlier variants primarily relied on SMS interception, OTP theft, phishing interfaces, and call-forwarding manipulation. The new variant can also monitor user interactions within legitimate financial applications and capture PIN-like input via Accessibility Service abuse. Command and Control Infrastructure The latest GhostBat RAT variant uses a multi-channel command-and-control architecture that combines a conventional HTTPS backend with Firebase services and a configurable WebSocket tunnel. Compared with earlier variants, which relied more heavily on hardcoded infrastructure, the new implementation provides greater operational flexibility by allowing the attacker to modify backend addresses and enable or disable selected malware capabilities remotely. In the analyzed sample, the default C&C infrastructure was configured as hxxps://api[.]cloudsettle[.]org. The malware communicates with this backend via multiple REST API endpoints that handle device registration, SMS collection, call log collection, command acknowledgement, PIN data submission, service state reporting, and other post-compromise functionality. Endpoint Purpose /sms/batch Uploads batches of SMS messages collected from the infected device /sms/new Sends newly received SMS messages to the C&C in near real time /sms/delivery-status Reports the delivery or failure status of remotely sent SMS messages /call-logs/batch Uploads collected call-log records in bulk /call-logs/new Sends newly observed call-log entries to the C&C /devices/sim-info Sends SIM and telephony-related information from the infected device /devices/update-token Registers or updates the device's Firebase Cloud Messaging token /devices/service-status Reports the operational status of malware services running on the device /commands/ack Acknowledges receipt or execution of commands issued by the C&C /commands/call-forward/status Reports the result or current state of call-forwarding operations /ping-response Responds to C&C ping requests and confirms that the infected device is online /upload-response Returns the result or status of generic upload or command operations /pin-data Uploads captured PIN-related data, including Ghost Overlay and broader PIN-capture records /live-keylog/status Reports or manages the operational state of the live keylogging functionality One of the major changes in the latest GhostBat RAT variant is the use of Firebase Remote Config as an additional control layer. The analyzed payload is associated with the Firebase project andromeda-d389d and retrieves remotely managed configuration values that control both infrastructure and malware functionality. Of particular interest is the base_url parameter, which allows the operator to replace the active REST backend without modifying or redistributing the APK. Therefore, api.cloudsettle.org represents the observed/default backend for this sample rather than a permanently fixed C&C address. Figure 17 – Dynamic C&C implementation A similar dynamic C&C approach was observed during the GhostX investigation. An earlier NextGen mParivahan sample associated with the ghostx-panel Firebase project retrieved its backend configuration from Firestore using the app_config/network document and the baseUrl field. In addition to the newly introduced Accessibility Service abuse, Ghost Overlay, targeted PIN capture, and dynamically configurable C&C functionality, GhostBat RAT continues to exhibit several core behaviors documented in our earlier research. These include collecting SMS messages from compromised devices, monitoring newly received messages for banking- and OTP-related content, stealing UPI credentials through fraudulent mParivahan payment interfaces, and registering compromised devices with attacker-controlled infrastructure. Earlier GhostBat RAT variants also used Telegram bots for device registration and operator notification, while selected dropper chains contained cryptocurrency-mining functionality alongside the information-stealing payload. These previously documented capabilities remain important to the overall GhostBat RAT operation; however, the latest variants significantly expand the malware's financial-theft and remote-control functionality. Rather than repeating the earlier functionality in detail, this analysis focuses on newly observed capabilities and architectural changes, particularly Accessibility Service abuse, Ghost Overlay PIN interception, broader targeting of financial applications, dynamic Firebase-based configuration, and evolving loader and C2 mechanisms. Conclusion The latest GhostBat RAT activity highlights continued evolution across both delivery mechanisms and post-compromise capabilities. The investigation into mParivahan- and eChallan-themed malware exposed the broader GhostX ecosystem, linking phishing infrastructure, backend control, and evolving GhostBat RAT payloads. The introduction of Accessibility Service abuse, Ghost Overlay, broader PIN capture, and Firebase-driven dynamic configuration significantly expands the malware’s financial-theft capabilities while making the operation more adaptable. Combined with continuously evolving loaders and active phishing activity, GhostBat RAT remains a threat to Android users, particularly across India’s banking, UPI, and digital payment ecosystem. Cyble’s Threat Intelligence Platforms continuously monitor emerging threats, infrastructure, and activity across the dark web , deep web , and open sources. This proactive intelligence empowers organizations with early detection, impersonation, infrastructure mapping, and attribution insights. Altogether, these capabilities provide a critical head start in mitigating and responding to evolving cyber threats . CRIL’s analysis of this campaign has been selected for the upcoming Association of Anti-Virus Asia Researchers (AVAR) conference, where these findings will be showcased. Our Recommendations We have listed essential cybersecurity best practices that form the first line of defense against attackers. We recommend that our readers follow the best practices given below: Install Apps Only from Trusted Sources: Download apps exclusively from official platforms like the Google Play Store . Avoid third-party app stores or links received via SMS, social media, or email. Be Cautious with Permissions and Installs: Never grant permissions and install an application unless you're certain of an app's legitimacy. Watch for Phishing Pages: Always verify the URL and avoid suspicious links and websites that ask for sensitive information. Enable Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA): Use MFA for banking and financial apps to add an extra layer of protection, even if credentials are compromised. Report Suspicious Activity: If you suspect you've been targeted or infected, report the incident to your bank and local authorities immediately. If necessary, reset your credentials and perform a factory reset. Use Mobile Security Solutions: Install a mobile security application that includes real-time scanning. Keep Your Device Updated: Ensure your Android OS and apps are updated regularly. Security patches often address vulnerabilities that malware exploits. MITRE ATT&CK® Techniques Tactic Technique ID Procedure Initial Access Phishing (T1660) GhostBat RAT is distributed through smishing messages containing malicious links that redirect victims to fake mParivahan/eChallan or Google Play-style pages used to deliver the malicious APK. Persistence Event Triggered Execution: Broadcast Receivers (T1624.001) GhostBat RAT uses a boot-triggered Broadcast Receiver to restart its malicious services and workers after device reboot, allowing the implant to resume background activity. Defense Evasion Masquerading: Match Legitimate Name or Location (T1655.001) GhostBat RAT masquerades as legitimate mParivahan/eChallan applications and uses government-themed names, icons, and interfaces to deceive victims. Defense Evasion Obfuscated Files or Information: Software Packing (T1406.002) GhostBat RAT uses multiple encrypted and packed loader mechanisms, including AES-CBC, XOR, SPKZ/SPK1, encrypted DEX stages, and the libnetbridge.so multi-stage loader to conceal the final payload. Defense Evasion Download New Code at Runtime (T1407) One observed GhostBat RAT delivery variant remotely downloads a second-stage APK, validates the payload, and installs it after the initial dropper executes. Defense Evasion Input Injection (T1516) GhostBat RAT abuses AccessibilityService.dispatchGesture() to replay intercepted PIN-keypad touches into legitimate Google Pay and MobiKwik applications as part of the Ghost Overlay technique. Credential Access Abuse Accessibility Features (T1453) The latest GhostBat RAT variant abuses Android Accessibility Service to monitor targeted financial applications, identify PIN-entry contexts, capture sensitive input, and support Ghost Overlay activity. Credential Access Input Capture: Keylogging (T1417.001) GhostBat RAT uses Accessibility Service events to capture PIN/key-input activity from targeted financial applications. The default configuration targets 60 Android banking, UPI, wallet, fintech, and payment applications. Credential Access Input Capture: GUI Input Capture (T1417.002) Selected GhostBat RAT variants use fraudulent payment interfaces to capture UPI PINs, payment-card details, and other financial information entered by victims. Credential Access Access Notifications (T1517) Selected GhostBat RAT variants register a notification-listener service to monitor notifications generated by other applications, potentially exposing OTPs and other sensitive information. Discovery System Information Discovery (T1426) GhostBat RAT collects device information including Android version, device model, manufacturer, identifiers, and other system metadata. Discovery Software Discovery (T1418) GhostBat RAT can enumerate applications installed on the compromised device and uses package information to identify targeted banking and financial applications. Collection Protected User Data: SMS Messages (T1636.004) GhostBat RAT collects historical SMS messages and monitors newly received messages, including OTPs, banking alerts, and other sensitive message content. Collection Protected User Data: Call Log (T1636.002) GhostBat RAT collects call-history information and uploads historical and newly observed call-log records through its C2 infrastructure. Impact SMS Control (T1582) GhostBat RAT can receive attacker-defined SMS jobs and send messages through the infected device's SIM, allowing compromised devices to be used for remotely controlled SMS transmission and potentially further smishing activity. Impact Call Control (T1616) GhostBat RAT can manipulate and query call forwarding using USSD-based operations and report the forwarding state to its C2 infrastructure. Command and Control Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (T1437.001) GhostBat RAT communicates with its backend through HTTPS REST APIs and uses Firebase Cloud Messaging for command delivery. The latest variant also contains a configurable secure WebSocket communication channel.

Subsequent variants of Ghostbat RAT introduced XOR-encrypted custom containers, SPKZ/SPK1 packaging, split-APK delivery, dynamically loaded DEX components, and Java-based in-memory loaders.

One variant moved away from embedded payload delivery entirely. It operated as a remote downloader, retrieving a second-stage APK from remote infrastructure, validating its SHA-256 hash, and installing it through Android's package installation framework.

The most recent variant analyzed introduces a substantially more complex native loader implemented in libnetbridge.so. This loader combines multiple transformations, encryption, compression, and custom container stages before recovering the final GhostBat RAT payload.

This diversification indicates continued modification of the delivery layer while broadly retaining the malware's post-compromise objectives. Consequently, detections that focus only on the outer APK, the encrypted asset name, or a single unpacking routine are unlikely to provide durable coverage.

The GhostBat RAT loaders/droppers variants we observed are listed below:

Figure 7 – GhostBat RAT Loader variants

The most recent GhostBat RAT sample introduced a significantly more complex native unpacking mechanism.

Unlike earlier variants that relied primarily on Java-based loaders or comparatively straightforward XOR/AES routines, this variant stores the encrypted payload inside an opaque application asset, assets/isti52q4, while most of the unpacking logic is implemented in the native library libnetbridge.so.

The visible application code does not directly expose the final malicious functionality. Instead, execution transitions to the native loader, which processes the embedded asset through several sequential stages of transformation and decryption (see Figure 8).

Figure 8 – Latest native dropper unpacking chain

The first stage processes content within the encrypted asset file and derives values required for subsequent decoding. The resulting data is then passed through an RC4-like transformation before being processed through AES-256-GCM. This layered approach prevents the encrypted asset from being recovered using simple XOR or direct AES key extraction techniques that worked against earlier GhostBat RAT loaders.

Following successful decryption, the loader recovers an MSZ1-formatted intermediate object that is decompressed using zlib. The decompressed data contains an MSP1 container that packages the final Android application components.

The recovered payload consists of a split-APK application, including base.apk and split_config.dex.apk.

The executable malware code is primarily contained within the recovered split configuration DEX.

Unlike earlier samples, where the encrypted payload could be identified directly from ZIP headers or standard APK structures, the latest loader hides the final application behind several custom transformations before any recognizable Android package becomes available.

This significantly increases the effort required for automated unpacking and reduces the effectiveness of simple asset-scanning techniques.

Advanced GhostBat RAT Payload

GhostBat RAT has evolved from an Android SMS and information stealer into a modular remote-access and Banking Trojan.

Across the analyzed variants, the malware demonstrates capabilities for device profiling, SMS interception, remote SMS transmission, call-forwarding manipulation, payment-data theft, accessibility-based PIN capture, Firebase-driven command delivery, dynamic C&C configuration, and remote tunnelling.

In the new GhostBat RAT variant, we observed the introduction of Android Accessibility Service abuse, a technique commonly associated with modern Android Banking Trojans.

Earlier GhostBat RAT variants that we analyzed did not possess these capabilities during this investigation. The new variant uses Accessibility Service to monitor foreground applications, identify PIN-entry contexts, interact with application interfaces, and support two distinct credential-theft mechanisms: Ghost Overlay and targeted PIN/key-input capture.

Once Accessibility Services access is granted, the malware monitors the foreground application and compares it against configured target lists. These targets can be managed through Firebase Remote Config, allowing operators to selectively activate credential-capture functionality when a targeted banking, UPI, wallet, or payment application is in use.

Ghost Overlay

The most notable capability introduced in this variant is the Ghost Overlay technique.

Figure 9.1 – Ghost Overlay Attack Flow

Unlike conventional Android overlay attacks that display a fake login or payment page over the legitimate application, GhostBat RAT does not need to replace the victim's banking interface. Instead, it places transparent accessibility overlay regions directly over the real PIN keypad displayed by the targeted application.

The feature is controlled through Firebase Remote Config using:

ghost_overlay_enabled

ghost_overlay_packages

Figure 9.2 – Ghost overlay initialization activity

The default Ghost Overlay configuration targets the following Android packages:

com.mobikwik_new

com.google.android.apps.nbu.paisa

com.google.android.apps.nbu.paisa.user

Figure 10 – Target package list of Ghost Overlay activity

When the malware detects one of these applications in the foreground and identifies a PIN-related activity, it creates a transparent keypad grid using Android’s TYPE_ACCESSIBILITY_OVERLAY. The overlay contains 12 touch regions matching the layout of a typical numeric PIN pad (see Figures 11 and 12):

Figure 11 – Ghost PIN pad structure

Figure 12 – Ghost overlay activity

When the victim taps a digit on the legitimate Google Pay or MobiKwik PIN keypad, the transparent Ghost Overlay intercepts the touch event before it reaches the underlying application.

The malware maps the touch coordinates to the corresponding keypad value and appends the resulting digit to an internal buffer used to reconstruct the PIN.

To avoid interrupting the payment flow or alerting the victim, GhostBat RAT temporarily releases the affected overlay region and uses AccessibilityService.dispatchGesture() to reproduce the same tap at the corresponding screen coordinates (see Figure 13).

As a result, the legitimate application receives the expected input and continues operating normally, while the malware records the victim's PIN in parallel.

The same mechanism handles DEL and OK interactions, allowing the GhostBat RAT to update the captured digit sequence and detect when the PIN entry process has completed. This intercept-and-replay behavior enables the malware to observe PIN entry without presenting a fake Google Pay or MobiKwik interface.

Figure 13 – dispatchGesture activity

Once collected, the PIN is stored with metadata identifying the capture source as ghost_overlay and is subsequently queued for exfiltration over C&C “hxxps://api.cloudsettle[.]org/pin-data” (see Figure 14).

Figure 14 – Storing captured Ghost PIN

This technique is considerably stealthier than a conventional phishing overlay because the victim remains within the genuine financial application's interface throughout the interaction. GhostBat RAT effectively operates as an invisible intermediary, intercepting the victim's keypad interaction, recording the selected digits, and replaying those same touches into the legitimate application in near real time.

Targeted Keylogging and PIN Capture

In addition to the Ghost Overlay capability, the new GhostBat RAT variant implements a broader accessibility-based PIN/key-input capture mechanism targeting applications across India’s banking, UPI, wallet, fintech, and digital-payment ecosystem.

Unlike the Ghost Overlay feature, which is specifically designed to intercept keypad touches in Google Pay and MobiKwik via transparent overlay regions, this functionality relies on Android Accessibility Service events to monitor user interactions across a much larger set of targeted applications.

The default pin_target_packages configuration includes 60 Android package identifiers for financial applications used across India (see Figure 15).

The target set includes applications associated with Google Pay, PhonePe, Paytm, MobiKwik, BHIM, SBI UPI, Axis Pay, BharatPe, CRED, Freecharge, PayZapp, Groww, Navi, Jupiter, OneCard, JioFinance, Samsung Pay, and several other banking and payment services. The complete list of targeted Android packages is provided in the Targeted Application List section.

Once Accessibility Service is granted, GhostBat RAT monitors foreground activity and determines whether the currently running application(s) match an entry in pin_target_packages. The malware then evaluates the surrounding application and screen context before treating observed numeric input as potentially sensitive PIN information.

Figure 15 – PIN target package list

The malware also uses configurable PIN-length boundaries, pin_min_digits, and pin_min_digits to determine whether the reconstructed numeric sequence is consistent with an expected PIN.

Unlike Ghost Overlay, the broader keylogging mechanism does not rely on a transparent keypad overlay. Instead, GhostBat RAT uses Accessibility Service events and UI context to identify and reconstruct PIN-like input across a wider set of targeted financial applications, giving the malware substantially broader coverage within India’s banking and digital payment ecosystem.

The analyzed variant contains a dedicated worker responsible for handling captured PIN information, “PinUploadWorker”. Captured PINS are locally queued before being transmitted to the endpoint “/pin-data”.

Figure 16 – Captured PIN upload activity

The introduction of this capability substantially expands the financial targeting of GhostBat RAT. Earlier variants primarily relied on SMS interception, OTP theft, phishing interfaces, and call-forwarding manipulation.

The new variant can also monitor user interactions within legitimate financial applications and capture PIN-like input via Accessibility Service abuse.

Command and Control Infrastructure

The latest GhostBat RAT variant uses a multi-channel command-and-control architecture that combines a conventional HTTPS backend with Firebase services and a configurable WebSocket tunnel.

Compared with earlier variants, which relied more heavily on hardcoded infrastructure, the new implementation provides greater operational flexibility by allowing the attacker to modify backend addresses and enable or disable selected malware capabilities remotely.

In the analyzed sample, the default C&C infrastructure was configured as hxxps://api[.]cloudsettle[.]org. The malware communicates with this backend via multiple REST API endpoints that handle device registration, SMS collection, call log collection, command acknowledgement, PIN data submission, service state reporting, and other post-compromise functionality.

Endpoint Purpose /sms/batch Uploads batches of SMS messages collected from the infected device /sms/new Sends newly received SMS messages to the C&C in near real time /sms/delivery-status Reports the delivery or failure status of remotely sent SMS messages /call-logs/batch Uploads collected call-log records in bulk /call-logs/new Sends newly observed call-log entries to the C&C /devices/sim-info Sends SIM and telephony-related information from the infected device /devices/update-token Registers or updates the device's Firebase Cloud Messaging token /devices/service-status Reports the operational status of malware services running on the device /commands/ack Acknowledges receipt or execution of commands issued by the C&C /commands/call-forward/status Reports the result or current state of call-forwarding operations /ping-response Responds to C&C ping requests and confirms that the infected device is online /upload-response Returns the result or status of generic upload or command operations /pin-data Uploads captured PIN-related data, including Ghost Overlay and broader PIN-capture records /live-keylog/status Reports or manages the operational state of the live keylogging functionality

One of the major changes in the latest GhostBat RAT variant is the use of Firebase Remote Config as an additional control layer. The analyzed payload is associated with the Firebase project andromeda-d389d and retrieves remotely managed configuration values that control both infrastructure and malware functionality.

Of particular interest is the base_url parameter, which allows the operator to replace the active REST backend without modifying or redistributing the APK. Therefore, api.cloudsettle.org represents the observed/default backend for this sample rather than a permanently fixed C&C address.

Figure 17 – Dynamic C&C implementation

A similar dynamic C&C approach was observed during the GhostX investigation. An earlier NextGen mParivahan sample associated with the ghostx-panel Firebase project retrieved its backend configuration from Firestore using the app_config/network document and the baseUrl field.

In addition to the newly introduced Accessibility Service abuse, Ghost Overlay, targeted PIN capture, and dynamically configurable C&C functionality, GhostBat RAT continues to exhibit several core behaviors documented in our earlier research.

These include collecting SMS messages from compromised devices, monitoring newly received messages for banking- and OTP-related content, stealing UPI credentials through fraudulent mParivahan payment interfaces, and registering compromised devices with attacker-controlled infrastructure.

Earlier GhostBat RAT variants also used Telegram bots for device registration and operator notification, while selected dropper chains contained cryptocurrency-mining functionality alongside the information-stealing payload.

These previously documented capabilities remain important to the overall GhostBat RAT operation; however, the latest variants significantly expand the malware's financial-theft and remote-control functionality.

Rather than repeating the earlier functionality in detail, this analysis focuses on newly observed capabilities and architectural changes, particularly Accessibility Service abuse, Ghost Overlay PIN interception, broader targeting of financial applications, dynamic Firebase-based configuration, and evolving loader and C2 mechanisms.

Conclusion

The latest GhostBat RAT activity highlights continued evolution across both delivery mechanisms and post-compromise capabilities. The investigation into mParivahan- and eChallan-themed malware exposed the broader GhostX ecosystem, linking phishing infrastructure, backend control, and evolving GhostBat RAT payloads.

The introduction of Accessibility Service abuse, Ghost Overlay, broader PIN capture, and Firebase-driven dynamic configuration significantly expands the malware’s financial-theft capabilities while making the operation more adaptable. Combined with continuously evolving loaders and active phishing activity, GhostBat RAT remains a threat to Android users, particularly across India’s banking, UPI, and digital payment ecosystem.

Cyble’s Threat Intelligence Platforms continuously monitor emerging threats, infrastructure, and activity across the dark web, deep web, and open sources. This proactive intelligence empowers organizations with early detection, impersonation, infrastructure mapping, and attribution insights. Altogether, these capabilities provide a critical head start in mitigating and responding to evolving cyber threats.

CRIL’s analysis of this campaign has been selected for the upcoming Association of Anti-Virus Asia Researchers (AVAR) conference, where these findings will be showcased.

Our Recommendations

We have listed essential cybersecurity best practices that form the first line of defense against attackers. We recommend that our readers follow the best practices given below:

  • Install Apps Only from Trusted Sources:
    Download apps exclusively from official platforms like the Google Play Store. Avoid third-party app stores or links received via SMS, social media, or email.

  • Be Cautious with Permissions and Installs:
    Never grant permissions and install an application unless you're certain of an app's legitimacy.

  • Watch for Phishing Pages:
    Always verify the URL and avoid suspicious links and websites that ask for sensitive information.

  • Enable Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA):
    Use MFA for banking and financial apps to add an extra layer of protection, even if credentials are compromised.

  • Report Suspicious Activity:
    If you suspect you've been targeted or infected, report the incident to your bank and local authorities immediately. If necessary, reset your credentials and perform a factory reset.

  • Use Mobile Security Solutions:
    Install a mobile security application that includes real-time scanning.

  • Keep Your Device Updated:
     Ensure your Android OS and apps are updated regularly. Security patches often address vulnerabilities that malware exploits.

The default configuration targets 60 Android banking, UPI, wallet, fintech, and payment applications. Credential Access Access Notifications (T1517) Selected GhostBat RAT variants register a notification-listener service to monitor notifications generated by other applications, potentially exposing OTPs and other sensitive information. items.title: Fake Chrome App on Google Play Evades Detection and Reaches 100,000+ Downloads
items.summary: A fake Google Chrome app appeared on Google Play with a screenshot showing more than 100,000 downloads, raising fresh concerns about app checks and paid search results. The listing copied Chrome’s name, icon, and description, but its developer was Hizbartech rather than Google LLC. The app reportedly appeared above the real browser as a sponsored result. However, the download badge does not prove that 100,000 people installed it while it carried Chrome’s branding. Available reports also do not establish password theft, a banking Trojan, or a confirmed malware payload. Researchers at PiunikaWeb noted the deceptive app after a user on Reddit’s r/browsers community flagged it. Their October 14 report described an adware listing and said a search for the developer’s name still found it, although they could not reproduce the sponsored Chrome search result themselves. Fake Chrome App on Google Play PiunikaWeb traced the app to a game called Ball Bounce, which reportedly appeared in August before changing its branding in late September. Android Authority reported an August 22 listing and a September 30 change, while SammyGuru found an archive suggesting July availability. The exact launch date remains uncertain. The key concern is the change in identity. A listing that once presented itself as a game later borrowed the appearance of a trusted browser. Earlier coverage of malicious Google Play apps shows how apps can change after release, although those separate cases do not establish what this copycat contained. Fake Chrome app sitting at the top of the search results (Source – PiunikaWeb) The suspicious package identifier, com.ballbounce.Hizbartech , also linked the listing to its earlier game identity. Unlike an app’s visible name and icon, this identifier gave investigators another way to connect the two versions. It is a useful search clue for device checks, not proof of specific malicious functions. PiunikaWeb cited Reddit users who installed the 42 MB app and found a contacts-style interface with AI avatars rather than a browser. Android Authority described a chat app with prepared responses. These accounts explain the mismatch between the listing and its behavior, but they are not a published code review. No reviewed report supplied evidence of browser password theft, remote control, or hidden banking screens in this app. Past reporting on fake Chrome installation pages describes SpyNote delivered through lookalike websites, but that was a different campaign. Its capabilities and indicators should not be assigned to this Google Play listing. Likewise, saying the app “evaded detection” describes its apparent passage through store checks, not a verified technical method. What the App Actually Did The available evidence does not show encrypted payloads, checks for test devices, delayed code downloads, or an Android security flaw. The documented issue is impersonation and a reported sponsored placement. Later coverage said the listing appeared to have been removed. SammyGuru reported that its link returned a not-found message on October 14, but cautioned that this did not confirm worldwide removal. It also found conflicting download figures: 100,000+ in a screenshot and 10,000+ in an indexed listing. These limits matter because install totals, store availability, and confirmed infections are different measures. Reporting on Google Play stealth loaders explains a separate method involving fake updates and later malware delivery. There is no published evidence connecting that technique or the Anatsa banking Trojan to Hizbartech’s app. Researchers searched for the app by entering the developer’s name, Hizbartech, the listing showed right up (Source – PiunikaWeb) Users should check that the official Chrome listing names Google LLC as its publisher and uses com.android.chrome as its package identifier. Anyone who installed the Hizbartech copy should remove it and run Google Play Protect. A familiar icon, sponsored placement, or large download badge should not replace checking the developer. For security teams, the package name offers a clearer starting point than searching only for Chrome. Review affected devices for the listed app and unexpected permissions, while keeping any findings separate from confirmed data theft. The public record still leaves that question unanswered. items.title: Multiple Active Directory Vulnerabilities Let Attackers Bypass Security Feature Remotely
items.summary: Microsoft has disclosed three Active Directory vulnerabilities that could let a remote attacker bypass a key security feature in Windows domain environments. The issues are tracked as CVE-2026-69982, CVE-2026-96252, and CVE-2026-108131, and administrators should review Microsoft’s Security Update Guide entries and deploy the available fixes as soon as possible. Active Directory is the central identity service many organizations use to manage users, computers, permissions, and access to business systems. A weakness that bypasses a security control in this environment can be serious because domain services sit at the center of authentication and trust. If an attacker can reach an exposed or poorly protected domain service, they may be able to weaken protections that are meant to block unauthorized activity. Microsoft has classified the three issues as security feature bypass vulnerabilities. This means the flaws do not necessarily give an attacker full control of a server. Instead, they may let an attacker bypass protections that would normally limit access, validate requests, or prevent unsafe behavior. Multiple Active Directory Vulnerabilities Security teams should treat this as a high-priority patching event, especially in networks where many internal systems can reach Active Directory services. The disclosed CVEs affect Microsoft Active Directory-related components , according to the vendor’s Security Update Guide pages. Microsoft’s public entries should be the source of truth for affected products, update packages, severity ratings, and mitigation guidance because details can change as the company publishes more information. Organizations should also confirm that all domain controllers and supporting Windows servers have received the latest cumulative updates. The remote nature of these flaws increases the concern for large enterprise networks. Attackers who already have a foothold in a network often look for ways to move toward domain controllers, where they can target identity systems and gain broader access. A security feature bypass could support that process by helping an intruder avoid a control that would otherwise stop or detect suspicious activity. Administrators should first identify every domain controller, including older systems, backup domain controllers, and systems in remote offices. Test patch deployment in a controlled group where possible, then roll it out quickly across production servers. Teams should verify successful installation through their endpoint management platform or Windows update reporting, rather than assuming that an update was applied. Network controls remain important during patching. Domain controller services should not be exposed directly to the public internet. Organizations should limit which hosts can communicate with directory services, separate administrative systems from user networks, and require strong authentication for privileged accounts. Organizations should also review monitoring tools for unusual authentication failures, unexpected privilege changes, new service accounts, or suspicious activity involving domain controllers. This update is another reminder that identity infrastructure needs the same urgent patching process as public-facing applications. Organizations have repeatedly faced serious risk from flaws in network and identity products, including recently disclosed issues affecting remote-access infrastructure such as Citrix NetScaler and Gateway vulnerabilities . Security teams can also review broader coverage of Microsoft security vulnerabilities to track related Windows and enterprise software updates. Microsoft has not provided evidence in the accessible update information that these specific flaws are being actively exploited. Still, defenders should not wait for confirmed exploitation before applying updates. Security feature bypass bugs can become more valuable when combined with credential theft, phishing, lateral movement, or another vulnerability. Organizations should review Microsoft’s advisories for CVE-2026-69982 , CVE-2026-96252 , and CVE-2026-108131 and confirm that all relevant Active Directory systems are updated. A weakness that bypasses a security control in this environment can be serious because domain services sit at the center of authentication and trust. If an attacker can reach an exposed or poorly protected domain service, they may be able to weaken protections that are meant to block unauthorized activity.

Microsoft has classified the three issues as security feature bypass vulnerabilities. This means the flaws do not necessarily give an attacker full control of a server. Instead, they may let an attacker bypass protections that would normally limit access, validate requests, or prevent unsafe behavior.

Multiple Active Directory Vulnerabilities

Security teams should treat this as a high-priority patching event, especially in networks where many internal systems can reach Active Directory services. The disclosed CVEs affect Microsoft Active Directory-related components, according to the vendor’s Security Update Guide pages.

Microsoft’s public entries should be the source of truth for affected products, update packages, severity ratings, and mitigation guidance because details can change as the company publishes more information.

Organizations should also confirm that all domain controllers and supporting Windows servers have received the latest cumulative updates.

The remote nature of these flaws increases the concern for large enterprise networks. Attackers who already have a foothold in a network often look for ways to move toward domain controllers, where they can target identity systems and gain broader access.

A security feature bypass could support that process by helping an intruder avoid a control that would otherwise stop or detect suspicious activity.

Administrators should first identify every domain controller, including older systems, backup domain controllers, and systems in remote offices. Test patch deployment in a controlled group where possible, then roll it out quickly across production servers.

Teams should verify successful installation through their endpoint management platform or Windows update reporting, rather than assuming that an update was applied.

Network controls remain important during patching. Domain controller services should not be exposed directly to the public internet. Organizations should limit which hosts can communicate with directory services, separate administrative systems from user networks, and require strong authentication for privileged accounts.

Organizations should also review monitoring tools for unusual authentication failures, unexpected privilege changes, new service accounts, or suspicious activity involving domain controllers. This update is another reminder that identity infrastructure needs the same urgent patching process as public-facing applications.

Organizations have repeatedly faced serious risk from flaws in network and identity products, including recently disclosed issues affecting remote-access infrastructure such as Citrix NetScaler and Gateway vulnerabilities.

Security teams can also review broader coverage of Microsoft security vulnerabilities to track related Windows and enterprise software updates. Microsoft has not provided evidence in the accessible update information that these specific flaws are being actively exploited.

Still, defenders should not wait for confirmed exploitation before applying updates. Security feature bypass bugs can become more valuable when combined with credential theft, phishing, lateral movement, or another vulnerability.

Organizations should review Microsoft’s advisories for CVE-2026-69982, CVE-2026-96252, and CVE-2026-108131 and confirm that all relevant Active Directory systems are updated.

items.title: Cisco Secure Email Gateway 0-Day Vulnerability Actively Exploited in Attacks
items.summary: Cisco has warned that attackers are actively exploiting a critical zero-day vulnerability in Cisco Secure Email Gateway that can give them root access to affected appliances. Tracked as CVE-2026-76519, the flaw carries a CVSS score of 9.8 and allows attacks through specially crafted email attachments without requiring a login. Cisco published its advisory on October 14, 2026. The company said its security response team became aware of active exploitation in October. Public reporting has not identified the attackers or established how many devices have been compromised, leaving the scale of the campaign unclear. The vulnerability sits in the Advanced Malware Protection feature, known as AMP. Cisco says the gateway fails to handle certain email attachments safely when its File Reputation service is enabled. An attacker can send a malicious attachment through an affected device to write arbitrary files and potentially execute commands with root privileges. Root access gives an attacker control over the underlying operating system. The entry point is the gateway processing an attachment, rather than a user opening a file. Cisco has not described a requirement for a recipient to click a link or launch the attachment. Cisco Secure Email Gateway 0-Day Vulnerability Both physical and virtual appliances are affected when they run vulnerable AsyncOS software and meet two conditions. File Reputation must be enabled and assigned to a mail policy, and the Content Scanner Tools package must be older than version 25.3.0.5525. Cisco Secure Email and Web Manager and Secure Web Appliance are not affected. This disclosure follows another actively exploited Secure Email Gateway flaw , CVE-2026-76461, reported in September. Earlier coverage of CVE-2025-20393 also documented attacks against Cisco email appliances, although that vulnerability involved the Spam Quarantine feature rather than AMP. Administrators can check File Reputation under the Advanced Malware Protection settings for incoming or outgoing mail policies. The contentscannerstatus command shows the installed Content Scanner Tools version. For investigation, Cisco recommends running grep "System Security" system_logs and checking every device in a cluster. A suspected compromise message requires incident response, while an incomplete security scan requires support from Cisco’s Technical Assistance Center. A clean result does not rule out an attack. Cisco warns that intruders with root access may hide or delete evidence. Security teams should also review independent firewall and network logs for unexpected uploads from the gateway or downloads from suspicious addresses. items.title: Detection engineering meets AI-driven adversary emulation
items.summary: In the first post in this series, Wade shared how our team laid the foundation for using AI in detection engineering. The short version is that an LLM doesn't know your stack. Without documentation and workflow context, it can produce plausible results that are difficult to trust, regardless of which model you use. That post closed with an instruction: Validate before you ship, because the output can look completely right and still be wrong. Every detection an agent writes still needs to go through the same review and testing as a human-written detection. Let’s discuss that last part, because it's harder than it sounds. We'd built a detection-as-code pipeline, and we were proud of it. Rules live in a repository. Changes arrive as pull requests, and they get peer-reviewed, planned, and applied through CI. We had the structure of a software engineering team, and we tested queries against the logs we had. For everything else, we had never watched the detections fire. We shipped those because they looked right. Validating a detection without the logs in your environment means running the attack technique yourself and watching it fire. We didn't have time to do that manually for every rule, and we had no automated way to do it. So here's the question. How many of your deployed detections have you watched fire? Not reviewed – actually watched fire . You don’t want to be answering that question the day an incident happens. Now that detections are code, they need to be tested like code. This post is about what it took to give our detections tests. An AI model did one job to make that possible, which is picking the attack technique to run against each detection. Why "it looks right" is not proof Before we get to the pipeline, it helps to see how a detection that looks right can still be broken. Reading a detection tells you what the query says, not what it actually does. It doesn't tell you whether the query matches any real logs, or whether the detection catches what you wrote it for. Here are five ways a detection can look right and still never fire: That field isn't what you think it is. It might have been renamed between vendor versions. It might be nested a level deeper than the docs suggest. Or it might be sitting in the raw message instead of parsed into a queryable attribute. The query is valid, it's just pointing at something that isn't there. Absence isn't emptiness. You write a condition for a field being missing, and the source sends it as an empty value instead of leaving it out. Depending on the query language, a wildcard matches that empty value, so the condition is never true and the rule never fires. The query language doesn't behave the way you read it. A quoted phrase doesn't always match the exact string you typed. Wildcards work one way on a parsed attribute and another way in free text. Case sensitivity or one unescaped character drops your result set to nothing. The data never reaches the query. The rule might be scoped to an index the logs don't route into. The source might have stopped shipping last week. Or an upstream parser change might have broken the field the rule depends on. The logic is fine. There's nothing for it to read. The threshold is set past what your environment can produce. If the most you've ever seen is ten events in a window and the rule fires at a hundred, you've written documentation, not a detection. Every one of these failures is silent. No error, nothing in the queue. A rule that can't fire looks exactly like a quiet environment. That reality is why "we have N detections" was never a coverage number. That number tells you how many rules you've written, not how many attack techniques you've proven you'd catch. These problems show up the first time you run the attack technique and check whether your detection fires. What this isn't We aren't a red team. I'm not a red teamer, and this isn't meant to replace one. Our approach starts from the detections we're writing or changing. For each one, AI picks the matching attack technique from a library of known techniques, the pipeline runs it, and then checks whether the detection’s query caught it. A red team tells you what you missed. This approach tests whether the detection you wrote works. This post also isn't an implementation guide. There's no code to copy. The emulation tooling we build on is open source, but the pipeline around it is our own. Instead, it covers why we built this, how the pieces fit together, and what we've learned running it. If you want the technical details, I'll be walking through them in a session at Datadog Detect in Chicago on November 2. Both sides of the test are code Detection-as-code is half of what makes this possible. The rules being tested are code. So is the thing doing the testing. Our attack library is a fork of Stratus Red Team , the open-source cloud adversary emulation project maintained by Datadog. Every technique is defined in that fork, released as pinned versions, and changed through pull requests like anything else. Because the catalog is code, the model mapping a rule to an attack technique gets a fixed list to choose from. Anything outside that list simply can't run. And if nothing in the catalog fits, the answer is no mapping, which is a useful answer in its own right. We fork instead of consuming upstream so we can add techniques for the behaviors we care about and control when the catalog changes. That gives us a versioned test input rather than an external dependency that can change without notice. A fork can also go stale. Keeping it synced is ongoing work, and if you skip it, your catalog quietly stops reflecting what techniques attackers actually use. That's part of the price. Our detections are code, and our attack library is code, which is the whole reason any of this can run in CI. You need both. Without an attack library, there's nothing to test your detections with. And if your detections live in a UI instead of code, there's nothing for CI to run the attack library against. The model’s one job The AI model has one job in this pipeline: mapping. It reads the whole detection, including the query, the MITRE ATT&CK tags, and the description, and picks the attack technique from our library that would trigger it. That's the hard part. The library labels each attack technique with a MITRE ATT&CK tactic, not a technique ID, so a detection's ATT&CK tag can't be matched against it directly. The query does most of the work, especially the event names it looks for, backed by a reference we wrote for each platform that maps common events to attack techniques. The tags and description add what the author meant to catch. It still takes judgment, and doing it by hand across hundreds of detections doesn't scale. Everything else is plain scripts. Running the attack technique, checking the SIEM, and posting the result on the pull request don't need judgment, so there's no reason to put a model where a script belongs. We also put guardrails on the model's answer. It has to reply in a fixed format that includes how confident it is, and it's told to return nothing rather than guess. A low-confidence answer gets treated the same as no answer, so a shaky guess never runs. Beyond the guardrails, we want to baseline the mapping against open-weight models. We'll give them the same detections we map today and see if they pick the same attack techniques, or if one model keeps favoring certain techniques or platforms. We also want to see whether a model's confidence score matches how often its picks actually pass. That tells us whether our results come from the context we built or from the model we happened to pick. What happens on a pull request When a pull request adds a detection, changes its query, or turns a disabled one back on, CI kicks off. Re-enabling counts because a rule that's been off is the one most likely to have gone stale. Edits that only touch tags, descriptions, or other metadata get skipped, since the logic didn't change. From there: The model maps the rule to an attack technique. The pipeline runs it in an isolated cloud environment with credentials pulled at runtime from our 1Password Connect server . A bot posts a pass or fail table back on the pull request. The attack technique runs for real. Nothing is replayed, and nothing is synthetic. What matters most is that your change isn't deployed yet. The pull request hasn't merged, so the SIEM is still running the old version of a rule you're modifying, and a rule you're creating isn't there at all. Either way, there's no signal from your version to wait for. So the pipeline runs the attack technique and then searches the logs with your query. That shows the events your rule is looking for actually landed, in the shape you expected, from a real attack technique. “Your logic matches reality" and "your detection works" are both worth having, but they aren't the same claim. Two details matter once you're running it. Threatest , an open-source detection testing framework also maintained by Datadog, runs the attack techniques from our library. Threatest can also check whether the SIEM caught one. We customized that check for our pipeline. Checking that matching logs showed up isn't enough on its own. Your query might match an earlier test, or other activity that happens to look the same. So every time the pipeline runs an attack technique, it stamps a unique ID into it, and validation looks for that ID in the logs your query returns. How much a green check proves Not every green check proves the same thing. There are two outcomes. The model mapped a technique. The pipeline ran the attack technique and found its events, with that run's unique ID in them, using the rule's own query. That's the strongest result a pull request can give you. The logic matches a real attack technique. Mapping takes judgment, so the model can still pick the wrong attack technique. When it does, your query won't find that technique's events and the check fails. In our system, a wrong pick shows up as a failure, not a false pass. The attack technique either produced the events your query looks for or it didn't. Nothing mapped. There's no attack technique to run, so the pipeline searches the last 30 days of logs with each of the rule's queries. If every query the rule needs matches at least once, it passes. That tells you the logic matches something real. It doesn't tell you it fires on the right thing. The split exists because cloud platforms can be attacked on demand and most SaaS sources can't. You can't safely make a third party's audit log produce an arbitrary event, so most SaaS rules never get a technique. SaaS is most of what most teams monitor, so most rules land in the second outcome. That's still better than shipping on "it looks right," but it's worth knowing which check you got. A green check that means " this could match " isn't the same as one that means " this matched an attack technique the pipeline just ran. " Where it falls short Some rules don't get a check at all, and that's a limitation we’ve accepted. Anomaly, new-value, and correlation rules get skipped. The first two need a baseline that one attack technique can't build, and correlation rules depend on other rules firing first. The check is advisory. A failed check shows up on the pull request, but it won't stop the merge. A CI error or an expired cloud credential shouldn't be able to keep a detection from shipping. The tradeoff is that nothing forces anyone to act on a failure, so we read every result as part of review. When a check fails, we don't merge until we know why. It's often one of the problems from earlier in this post, like a field that isn't where the query expects it or data that never reaches the index. The author pushes a fix to the same pull request, and the check runs again. If the model picked the wrong attack technique, the result shows that too, because the table names the technique it ran. It only runs on pull requests. A detection gets tested when someone changes its query or turns it back on, and deployed detections that nobody touches never get retested.
